land.text: Jambi, annexed into the Palembang Residency in 1903; Sultan Taha killed in 1904

successors.note: Jambi page: annexed into the Palembang Residency in 1903, and the death of Taha in 1904 marked the end of the sultanate.

capitals.name: Tanah Pilih (Jambi)
capitals.note: The infobox lists Tanah Pilih as capital with no years; the text has Lower Jambi based there after 1688. Coordinates are the gazetteer's Jambi (city); the pages give none, and the earlier seat of the 1460 kingdom is not named.

correction.text: the Cliopatria 1670 shape reused for the earlier life: the page describes the kingdom and sultanate only by their river domain ('Jambi with its nine rivers', directly administered along the Batanghari, part of the Tembesi and Tungkal)

keyframe_review.note: New keyframe: Cliopatria's first shape begins in 1670 but the page gives a Kingdom (1460-1615) and Sultanate (1615-1904), and the Datuk Puduko Berhalo page dates the first king to 1460. No page gives an extent before 1670; the 1670 shape is the best available, so treat 1460-1654 as soft. Revised after review: the 1670 shape includes the Tungkal coast, which a pro-Johor rebellion took from Jambi in 1655, so this keyframe now ends in 1654 and the next one (sultanate-of-jambi_1655) removes Tungkal. The Johor-Jambi wars page gives no year for Jambi's seizure of Tungkal ('Jambi took advantage of the Acehnese invasion of Johor to seize Tungkal'), so Tungkal may not have been Jambi's for the earliest years of 1460-1654.

minus.text: Tungkal, which 'a pro-Johorese rebellion forced' Jambi out of in 1655

correction.text: Tungkal remained under Jambian sovereignty 'until a pro-Johorese rebellion forced them out in 1655': Cliopatria's 1670 shape without the 60 km Tungkal disc (83 of its 101 cells), until the recapture c. 1681

keyframe_review.note: New keyframe added after review. The 1670 shape and the 1460-1669 keyframe both kept Tungkal while the ledger loses it in 1655 and regains it c. 1681; the disc covers 18 of the shape's 101 cells (about 4,550 km2, 18 percent), too large to leave undrawn. The year of the recapture is the page's silence: it follows the 1679 Johorese attack in the page text, but the infobox lists the recapture of Kuala Tungkal among the results of the 1673 war and a fourth war in 1680-1681, so 1680 as the last year is a bridge (confidence 1). Cliopatria's 1670 shape (next entry) therefore holds from c. 1681.

Adjusted after review (was ok): the years change, not the outline. 27,697 km2 (about 24.5 k km2 on the grid, roughly the eastern half of Jambi province) for 1670-1821. The page gives no infobox area, so no ratio could be taken. It describes the direct domain as the Jambian Malays along the Batanghari and part of the Tembesi, and Tungkal (page wording), with Sungai Tenang, Serampas and (from the mid-18th century) Kerinci autonomous: a lowland shape without the highlands fits that. The shape includes the Tungkal coast, which Johor held from 1655 until the undated recapture c. 1681 (Johor-Jambi wars page); 1670-1680 is drawn without it in sultanate-of-jambi_1655.

correction.text: shape unchanged, but it holds from c. 1681, when Tungkal returns; for 1670-1680 the shape is the keyframe sultanate-of-jambi_1655 (the same outline without the Tungkal disc). Cliopatria dates it 1670-1821; the 1670 start is not supported by the page for the Tungkal coast

keyframe_review.note: 27,467 km2, 0.8% below the 1670 shape. No page explains the step; it coincides with the Dutch annexation of Palembang ('In 1821 the Dutch attacked Palembang again and annexed the city', Palembang page), after which Cliopatria's neighbour on this border is the Dutch East Indies, so it is read as a clipping against that shape. The Jambi page has nothing on Jambi territory in 1822.

27,150 km2, 1.1% below the 1822 shape, the western edge moving about 9 km east. The Jambi page names no 1895 event (it jumps from the 1858 Dutch expedition and Dutch-backed sultans to the 1899 abdication of Zainuddin); unverified: page silent. Cliopatria lists the Qajar Dynasty as a neighbour in 1895-1897, an artifact of its data.

Same outline as 1895-1899 (27,150 km2). 1900: Taha 'became sultan for a second time' (Thaha page) and fought the Dutch to his death in 1904; the Jambi page has the sultanate annexed into the Palembang Residency in 1903. The shape is the sultanate as the pages' claim, not the ground the Dutch held, which they controlled in much of it from 1858.

region.text: the Jambi lowlands on the Batanghari; 'In 1460 AD, Datuk Paduko reigned as Berhalo'

ledger.note: 1460: Datuk Paduko Berhalo founds the Kingdom of Jambi. The Datuk page has him ruling 1460-1480 as the founder and first king of the Kingdom of Jambi; the Jambi Sultanate infobox reads 'Kingdom (1460-1615); Sultanate (1615-1904)'. The Jambi page also says Jambi was part of Majapahit from the mid-14th century and broke away in the early 16th, which does not fit a 1460 founding; the page does not reconcile the two, so the year is the pages' and the land is the researcher's reading (counterpart nobody: Majapahit's hold is unclear).

c. 1615: the kingdom becomes a sultanate. 'At around 1615, Jambi became a sultanate'; the English and Dutch trading posts date to the same time and by 1616 Jambi was 'the second-largest Sumatran port after Aceh'.

region.text: Tungkal, which a pro-Johor rebellion forced Jambi out of in 1655

ledger.note: 1655: Tungkal passes from Jambi to Johor. the Johor-Jambi wars page lists 1655: a pro-Johor rebellion forced Jambi out of Tungkal; in 1629 Johor had asked for Tungkal back and Jambi kept it. The page does not say Johor annexed it; the Johor dossier records the same event as a gain. Drawn in the keyframe sultanate-of-jambi_1655 (the 1670 shape without the Tungkal disc).

region.text: Tungkal and the lower Indragiri, where the page has the raids and the recapture (the same Tungkal disc as the Johor dossier; the lower Indragiri is the river's last 60 km round its mouth)

ledger.note: May 1667: the Johor-Jambi war begins at sea and on the coast. the page's May 1667 entry: a Johorese fleet destroyed fishing huts and orchards at the mouth of the Jambi River; the page puts the first clash near Lingga in 1666 (with Palembang) and the Jambi raid on Indragiri and Tungkal in August 1670. Same date as the Johor dossier. Zone revised after review: the page names fighting only at the mouth of the Jambi River (a Johorese sea raid, May 1667), at Indragiri and Tungkal (Jambian raids, August 1670) and at Jambi (May 1679), nothing up the Indragiri valley, so the earlier 20 km buffer along the whole Batang Indragiri (about 17,450 km2) is replaced by the river's last 60 km round its mouth (103.35 E, 0.30 S, the end of the gazetteer's river line). The Jambi River mouth is not drawn: the gazetteer has no Batang Hari and the page records a sea raid, not land held. The Johor dossier still carries the old specification (sultanate-of-johor /ledger/11 and /ledger/13).

region.text: Tungkal and the lower Indragiri, where the page has the raids and the recapture (the same Tungkal disc as the Johor dossier; the lower Indragiri is the river's last 60 km round its mouth)

ledger.note: 1679-1681: the war ends with Jambi back on its coast. in May 1679 Johor attacked Jambi with 300 ships and Jambi paid 10,000 rijksdaalders and sent two hostages; then, with VOC support, Jambi recaptured Kuala Tungkal and Indragiri and Daeng Mangika was killed (undated; the page's infobox lists a fourth war 1680-1681 as a Jambi victory). The Johor dossier ends the contest on 17 October 1679; the end year here is the infobox's, so confidence 1. Zone revised after review as for the 1667 contest_start (Tungkal and the lower Indragiri only).

region.text: Kuala Tungkal, 'recaptured' by Jambi; the Tungkal disc within the 1670 shape, the same land lost in 1655

ledger.note: c. 1681: Jambi recovers Tungkal. The Johor-Jambi wars page says Jambi 'unexpectedly countered the Johor-Palembang-Bugis attacks and recaptured Kuala Tungkal and Indragiri' and its text ends the war on that recapture. The page gives no year (the infobox lists 'Recapture of Kuala Tungkal' among the results of the 1673 war and a fourth war 1680-1681 as a Jambi victory), so 1681 is a bridge (confidence 1). Revised after review: only the land lost in 1655 (the Tungkal disc within the 1670 shape, 18 cells) is drawn as regained. The recapture of Indragiri is not drawn: the page never says Jambi held Indragiri before (the Jambi Sultanate page has Jambi attacking Indragiri in August 1670 and after the 1673 sack, 'although Indragiri managed to hold its own'), it does not name a former holder, and its infobox gives the territorial change as 'status quo ante bellum'; the Jambi page describes the domain as the Batanghari, part of the Tembesi and Tungkal. The counterpart is Johor as the holder of Tungkal since 1655; the page does not say who held it in 1681, so the Johor dossier needs a matching c. 1681 loss of Tungkal or the same silence.

region.text: Upper Jambi, upstream of Lower Jambi at Tanah Pilih

ledger.note: 1688: the VOC deposes Sultan Ingalaga and Jambi divides. The page says the VOC arrested and deposed Sultan Ingalaga and Jambi split into Lower Jambi (Tanah Pilih, under the VOC-backed Kiai Gede) and Upper Jambi (under Pringgabaya); Upper Jambi was under Pagaruyung's influence. The boundary between the halves is not on the page; the 60 km radius around Jambi city is the researcher's reading.

1708: Jambi is reunited. In 1708 Kiai Gede gave up his authority to Pringgabaya, reuniting Jambi (page wording, closely paraphrased). The page adds that the sultanate was badly weakened by the decline of trade.

region.text: Upper Jambi, upstream of Lower Jambi: Taha 'fled upstream into the region of Upper Jambi'

ledger.note: 1858: a Dutch expedition deposes Sultan Taha and Jambi divides again. 'In 1858, an expedition was launched that deposed Sultan Taha within a day. He fled upstream into the region of Upper Jambi, while his uncle, Ahmad Nazaruddin, became the new ruler of Jambi. This divided Jambi into two competing areas: Upper and Lower, restoring a divide that had not existed since the early 18th century.' Lower Jambi was governed by Dutch-controlled shadow rulers (Ahmad Nazaruddin 1858-1881, Mohildin 1882-1885, Zainuddin 1886-1899), so it belongs to the Dutch East Indies dossier as a protectorate tint. The division is not ended by a merge: the Thaha page has Taha 'continue to claim the sultanate and to rule over its less accessible parts until he was killed by Dutch soldiers in 1904', while the Jambi page has Zainuddin forced to abdicate in 1899 and the Palembang resident holding the sultan's position until the 1903 annexation; the 1904 dissolve closes both halves (added after review). The boundary is not on the pages; the 60 km radius round Jambi city is the researcher's reading, as for 1688.

region.text: Jambi, annexed into the Palembang Residency in 1903

ledger.note: 1903-1904: the Dutch absorb Jambi. the page has Jambi annexed into the Palembang Residency in 1903; Taha was killed in 1904 (Thaha page: 'killed in 1904 by Dutch soldiers' at Betung Bedarah). The page does not say the Dutch took the whole shape on one date; the Dutch had deposed Taha in 1858 and set up sultans who 'reigned over much of the sultanate until 1899' (Thaha page).

1904: the Jambi Sultanate ends with the death of Sultan Taha. the page says Taha's killing marked the end of the sultanate; infobox 'Disestablished: 1904'; a caption dates the crown prince's surrender of the insignia to 26 March 1904.

wars.name: Johor-Jambi wars

zones.text: Tungkal and the lower Indragiri, where the page has the raids and the recapture (the same Tungkal disc as the Johor dossier; the lower Indragiri is the river's last 60 km round its mouth)

wars.outcome: Jambi burned Johor's capital on 4 April 1673 and was beaten in 1679 (300 Johor ships; 10,000 rijksdaalders, two cannons and two hostages); with VOC help it then recovered Kuala Tungkal and Indragiri and Daeng Mangika was killed. The war ended Jambi's role as a major pepper port.
wars.note: The page's infobox dates the war 1711-1718, which its own text contradicts; the years here are the body's (1666 to 1681). Four phases in the infobox: 1667 (Johor), 1673 (Jambi), 1677-1679 (Johor), 1680-1681 (Jambi). The Johor dossier cites the Jambi Sultanate page for the same war and ends it in October 1679. Zone revised after review: the page names fighting only at the mouth of the Jambi River (a Johorese sea raid, May 1667), at Indragiri and Tungkal (Jambian raids, August 1670) and at Jambi (May 1679), nothing up the Indragiri valley, so the earlier 20 km buffer along the whole Batang Indragiri (about 17,450 km2) is replaced by the river's last 60 km round its mouth (103.35 E, 0.30 S, the end of the gazetteer's river line). The Jambi River mouth is not drawn: the gazetteer has no Batang Hari and the page records a sea raid, not land held. The Johor dossier still carries the old specification (sultanate-of-johor /ledger/11 and /ledger/13).

wars.name: Dutch conquest of Jambi
wars.outcome: 1833: Sultan Mohammad Fakhruddin invaded Dutch-controlled Palembang and was forced to accept Dutch authority and concessions; 1858: a Dutch expedition deposed Taha and installed Ahmad Nazaruddin; 1903: annexation into the Palembang Residency; 1904: Taha killed and the sultanate ends.
wars.note: The page names no treaty with a year. Taha also sought Ottoman help in 1857, 1902 and 1903, all in vain. From 1858 the Dutch-backed sultans 'reigned over much of the sultanate until 1899' while Taha ruled the inaccessible parts (Thaha page), so the border of Dutch control inside the shape is not on the pages. Zones emptied after review: the page gives no front line or contest, and the only border moves are in the ledger (the 1858 division of Jambi into Upper and Lower, and the 1904 loss to the Dutch East Indies), so no contest zone is claimed; the earlier zone was the whole 1900 shape with no contest_start or contest_end behind it.

certainty.note: A river domain ('Jambi with its nine rivers') whose upland edges (Sungai Tenang, Serampas, Kerinci) were autonomous; no treaty line is on the pages, even for the Dutch period.

notes: Life span: Cliopatria's row is 1670-1904; the Jambi Sultanate infobox gives Kingdom 1460-1615 and Sultanate 1615-1904, and the Datuk Puduko Berhalo page dates the first king to 1460, so the dossier starts in 1460 and records 1615 as a rename; the 1460-1669 keyframe reuses the Cliopatria 1670 shape because no page gives an earlier extent. Conflict inside the Jambi page: Jambi was part of Majapahit from the mid-14th century and broke away in the early 16th century, which does not fit a 1460 kingdom; a Majapahit dossier may carry a vassal or territorial claim over Jambi that overlaps 1460-c. 1520. Other relations on the Jambi page that the ledger types cannot express from Jambi's side (Jambi as the subordinate): 1642 Pangeran Ratu accepted Mataram's overlordship and Jambi broke away in 1663/64 (Mataram dossier: vassal_start/vassal_end with counterpart sultanate-of-jambi); by the end of the 18th century Jambi was a vassal of Pagaruyung and Upper Jambi was under Pagaruyung's influence in 1688 (Pagaruyung/Minangkabau needs a dossier from the additions batch); 1682 Jambi was disputed as a vassal between the VOC and Siam; 1833 the sultan was forced to accept Dutch authority and make economic concessions, and from 1858 the sultans were Dutch-backed (the Dutch East Indies dossier, se-03, should carry the protectorate). March 1768: a hundred men attacked the Dutch settlement on the Sultan's orders and the Dutch left by 1770 (no land change). Kerinci was autonomous from the mid-18th century (page gives no event). Johor-Jambi wars page: the Johor dossier (se-02) says 'No Wikipedia article Johor-Jambi War was found'; the article exists at https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Johor%E2%80%93Jambi_wars and dates the end of the fighting to 1680-1681 (infobox) rather than 1679. Cliopatria neighbours: Qajar Dynasty is listed 1895-1897, impossible; the Dutch East Indies neighbour is missing for those years. The gazetteer has no 'Batang Hari' river, 'Tungkal', 'Kerinci' or 'Tanah Pilih'; Tungkal is given by coordinates as in the Johor dossier. Revised 2026-10-19 after review (fail, four findings). (1) The c. 1681 gain no longer adds the Batang Indragiri valley: it is the Tungkal disc within the 1670 shape, the land lost in 1655; the page never says Jambi held Indragiri and gives 'status quo ante bellum' (the recapture of Indragiri is not drawn). (2) The contest zone is the Tungkal disc plus the river's last 60 km round the Indragiri mouth, not a buffer along the whole river; the Johor dossier (sultanate-of-johor /ledger/11 and /ledger/13) uses the old specification and needs the same change. (3) K0 now ends in 1654, a new keyframe sultanate-of-jambi_1655 draws 1655-1680 without Tungkal, and K1 is adjust (shape holds from c. 1681). The page gives no year for Jambi's seizure of Tungkal, so the earliest years of the 1670 shape used for 1460-1654 may include Tungkal too early. The year of the recapture is open: text after the 1679 attack, but the infobox lists the recapture of Kuala Tungkal under the 1673 war. (4) The 1858 division is added as a split (counterpart 'Upper Jambi (Sultan Taha)') closed by the 1904 dissolve, and the Dutch-conquest war has no zones. I disagree with nothing in the review; I chose the split rather than a contest 1858-1904 because the page itself says the expedition 'divided Jambi into two competing areas' and gives no front line. Note for the Dutch East Indies owner (se-03): Lower Jambi had Dutch-controlled shadow sultans from 1858 to 1899 and the Palembang resident as 'sultan' to 1903. Pages re-opened 2026-10-19: Jambi Sultanate, Johor-Jambi wars, Thaha Syaifuddin; the Indragiri Hilir Regency page was opened for coordinates and prints none (the Indragiri mouth comes from the gazetteer's river line).
